explainer.whatItIs: The pituitary's signal telling your thyroid how hard to work.
explainer.whyItMatters: It's the master dial for energy, metabolism, temperature and mood. High TSH usually means an underactive thyroid; low means overactive.
explainer.whatYoursSuggests: Comfortably mid-range — the pituitary isn't straining to push the thyroid, which is reassuring.

explainer.whatItIs: The 'storage' thyroid hormone circulating freely, ready to be converted to the active form.
explainer.whyItMatters: It's the reservoir your body draws on. Low levels can mean sluggish thyroid output.
explainer.whatYoursSuggests: Solidly in range — adequate hormone available to convert as needed.

explainer.whatItIs: The active thyroid hormone — the one that actually does the work in your cells.
explainer.whyItMatters: This is what drives day-to-day energy and metabolism. It reflects how well you convert T4 into the usable form.
explainer.whatYoursSuggests: Healthy mid-range conversion — your cells are getting the active hormone they need.

explainer.whatItIs: An inactive 'brake-pedal' version of thyroid hormone the body makes, often more under stress.
explainer.whyItMatters: When it climbs, it can blunt the effect of the active hormone even if other numbers look fine — a common stress/inflammation signal.
explainer.whatYoursSuggests: Sitting at the top of the range. Not alarming, but worth watching alongside stress and the active T3 number. One to track at the next draw.

markers.name: Thyroid Peroxidase Antibody (TPO)

explainer.whatItIs: An antibody that targets an enzyme inside the thyroid gland.
explainer.whyItMatters: Elevated TPO is the classic marker of autoimmune thyroid activity (Hashimoto's pattern) — the immune system nudging the thyroid. It doesn't necessarily mean symptoms today, but it explains why thyroid support is on the protocol.
explainer.whatYoursSuggests: Above the reference cutoff, consistent with an autoimmune thyroid picture. The current thyroid hormone numbers are still healthy, so this is about monitoring the trend rather than a crisis. Worth discussing with your doctor.

markers.labNote: Elevated anti-TPO antibodies are associated with autoimmune thyroid disease. Clinical correlation recommended.

explainer.whatItIs: A second thyroid antibody, this one against thyroglobulin, a protein the gland uses to make hormone.
explainer.whyItMatters: Alongside TPO, it reinforces the autoimmune thyroid pattern. Two positive antibodies is a clearer signal than one.
explainer.whatYoursSuggests: Elevated, mirroring the TPO result — together they paint a consistent autoimmune-thyroid story. Track over time; the support protocol (selenium, vitamin D) targets exactly this.

explainer.whatItIs: Blood sugar after an overnight fast — a snapshot of baseline glucose.
explainer.whyItMatters: Persistently high fasting glucose is an early sign of insulin resistance and metabolic strain.
explainer.whatYoursSuggests: Comfortably normal — no fasting-glucose red flag.

explainer.whatItIs: A 3-month average of blood sugar, read from sugar stuck to red blood cells.
explainer.whyItMatters: It smooths out daily noise and is the standard gauge for diabetes risk. 5.7–6.4% is pre-diabetes.
explainer.whatYoursSuggests: Well within the healthy band — your 3-month average blood sugar looks good.

explainer.whatItIs: How much insulin your pancreas is producing at rest.
explainer.whyItMatters: Insulin can run high years before glucose does — a low-normal value suggests your cells respond to insulin efficiently.
explainer.whatYoursSuggests: In the lower-normal zone, which generally points to good insulin sensitivity.

explainer.whatItIs: The sum of cholesterol carried in your blood.
explainer.whyItMatters: A blunt number on its own — the breakdown (LDL, HDL, triglycerides) matters more — but a useful headline.
explainer.whatYoursSuggests: Below the cutoff; the detailed lipid breakdown below tells the fuller story.

explainer.whatItIs: The 'delivery' cholesterol that can build up in artery walls when too high.
explainer.whyItMatters: It's the primary lipid target for cardiovascular risk.
explainer.whatYoursSuggests: Below the general threshold — a favourable number.

explainer.whatItIs: The 'cleanup' cholesterol that carries excess back to the liver.
explainer.whyItMatters: Higher is generally protective — this is one where you want to be above the floor.
explainer.whatYoursSuggests: Healthily above the minimum — a protective level.

explainer.whatItIs: Fat circulating in the blood, strongly tied to diet and carbohydrate load.
explainer.whyItMatters: High triglycerides track with insulin resistance and cardiovascular risk.
explainer.whatYoursSuggests: Low and healthy — consistent with the good metabolic markers.

explainer.whatItIs: A direct count of the artery-clogging particles, often more precise than LDL alone.
explainer.whyItMatters: Each harmful particle carries one ApoB, so it captures true particle burden.
explainer.whatYoursSuggests: In a favourable range — the particle count backs up the good LDL number.

explainer.whatItIs: An adrenal hormone that's a building block for other hormones and a rough adrenal-reserve gauge.
explainer.whyItMatters: It tends to fall with chronic stress and age; healthy levels support resilience and recovery.
explainer.whatYoursSuggests: Mid-range — adrenal reserve looks solid. Worth trending alongside reverse T3 and cortisol.

explainer.whatItIs: The primary androgen, affecting energy, muscle, libido and mood.
explainer.whyItMatters: Low levels can mean fatigue, low drive and poor recovery.
explainer.whatYoursSuggests: Comfortably mid-range — no concern here.

explainer.whatItIs: Your main stress hormone, measured in the morning when it should naturally peak.
explainer.whyItMatters: A healthy morning peak drives the wake-up and energy curve; chronically high or flat patterns signal stress-axis strain.
explainer.whatYoursSuggests: A normal morning level. The PM Cortisol Manager supplement is about smoothing the evening curve, not fixing a high number.

explainer.whatItIs: A liver enzyme that leaks into blood when liver cells are stressed.
explainer.whyItMatters: It's a sensitive flag for liver inflammation or fatty liver.
explainer.whatYoursSuggests: Normal — no sign of liver-cell stress.

explainer.whatItIs: A second liver/muscle enzyme, read alongside ALT.
explainer.whyItMatters: The AST:ALT ratio helps distinguish liver from muscle sources.
explainer.whatYoursSuggests: Normal and in line with ALT — a healthy liver picture.

explainer.whatItIs: An enzyme from liver, bile ducts and bone.
explainer.whyItMatters: Helps flag bile-flow issues or bone turnover when out of range.
explainer.whatYoursSuggests: Mid-range and unremarkable.

explainer.whatItIs: A liver enzyme sensitive to alcohol and bile-flow stress.
explainer.whyItMatters: A useful cross-check on the other liver enzymes and oxidative load.
explainer.whatYoursSuggests: Low-normal — no biliary or alcohol-related stress signal.

markers.name: Total Bilirubin

explainer.whatItIs: A yellow pigment from the normal recycling of old red blood cells, cleared by the liver.
explainer.whyItMatters: Mildly high bilirubin with otherwise normal liver enzymes is most often Gilbert's syndrome — a common, harmless inherited quirk in how bilirubin is processed.
explainer.whatYoursSuggests: Slightly above the cutoff but flagged benign: all other liver markers are normal, fitting the Gilbert's pattern. Not a cause for concern — confirm the interpretation with your doctor.

markers.labNote: Isolated elevation of unconjugated bilirubin with normal hepatic enzymes is consistent with Gilbert's syndrome.

explainer.whatItIs: The main protein the liver makes, a marker of liver synthesis and nutrition.
explainer.whyItMatters: Low albumin can reflect poor liver function, inflammation or malnutrition.
explainer.whatYoursSuggests: Healthy — good liver synthetic function and protein status.

explainer.whatItIs: A muscle-breakdown waste product the kidneys filter out.
explainer.whyItMatters: Rising creatinine signals the kidneys aren't clearing waste as well.
explainer.whatYoursSuggests: Normal — consistent with healthy kidney filtering.

explainer.whatItIs: A calculated estimate of how fast your kidneys filter blood.
explainer.whyItMatters: The headline number for overall kidney health; below 60 sustained warrants attention.
explainer.whatYoursSuggests: Well above the floor — kidney filtration looks strong.

explainer.whatItIs: The main electrolyte governing fluid balance.
explainer.whyItMatters: Tightly regulated; deviations can affect hydration, blood pressure and nerves.
explainer.whatYoursSuggests: Dead centre — well-regulated fluid balance.

explainer.whatItIs: An electrolyte critical for heart rhythm and muscle function.
explainer.whyItMatters: Both high and low levels can affect the heartbeat, so it's kept in a tight window.
explainer.whatYoursSuggests: Comfortably mid-range.

explainer.whatItIs: Your stored-iron gauge — the body's iron savings account.
explainer.whyItMatters: Low ferritin means depleted iron stores (fatigue, hair loss); very high can signal inflammation or overload.
explainer.whatYoursSuggests: Healthy stores — no iron-deficiency signal.

explainer.whatItIs: Iron currently circulating in the blood (distinct from stored iron).
explainer.whyItMatters: A point-in-time number that's read together with ferritin and TIBC.
explainer.whatYoursSuggests: Mid-range and consistent with the healthy ferritin.

explainer.whatItIs: How much capacity your blood has to carry iron — rises when iron is scarce.
explainer.whyItMatters: Helps interpret whether low iron is a supply or a transport issue.
explainer.whatYoursSuggests: Normal — no sign the body is scrambling for iron.

explainer.whatItIs: The percentage of your iron-transport capacity actually in use.
explainer.whyItMatters: Low suggests deficiency; high can hint at iron overload.
explainer.whatYoursSuggests: Right in the sweet spot — balanced iron transport.

markers.name: Vitamin D (25-OH)

explainer.whatItIs: The storage form of vitamin D, the standard measure of your vitamin D status.
explainer.whyItMatters: Beyond bones, vitamin D modulates the immune system — directly relevant to the autoimmune thyroid picture. Low levels are extremely common.
explainer.whatYoursSuggests: Below the sufficiency threshold. This is the most actionable flag here, and the Vitamin D & K2 supplement on the protocol targets it. Re-test after a few months of consistent dosing to confirm it's climbing.

markers.labNote: Levels below 75 nmol/L are considered insufficient by many guidelines. Supplementation and recheck may be appropriate.

explainer.whatItIs: A vitamin essential for nerves, energy and red blood cell production.
explainer.whyItMatters: Low B12 causes fatigue, brain fog and nerve symptoms.
explainer.whatYoursSuggests: Comfortably in range; the B12 supplement keeps it topped up.

explainer.whatItIs: A B-vitamin working with B12 on DNA, nerves and red blood cells.
explainer.whyItMatters: Adequate folate supports methylation and energy pathways.
explainer.whatYoursSuggests: Well above the floor — good folate status.

explainer.whatItIs: A mineral involved in hundreds of reactions — muscle, nerve, sleep and energy.
explainer.whyItMatters: Serum magnesium is a rough gauge (most is inside cells), but low values are still meaningful.
explainer.whatYoursSuggests: Mid-range; the PM magnesium supplement supports sleep and relaxation regardless.

explainer.whatItIs: A sensitive marker of low-grade, body-wide inflammation.
explainer.whyItMatters: Chronic inflammation links to cardiovascular and metabolic risk; under 1.0 mg/L is considered low risk.
explainer.whatYoursSuggests: Low — no signal of systemic inflammation, which is reassuring given the autoimmune antibodies.

explainer.whatItIs: The count of immune cells in your blood.
explainer.whyItMatters: High can mean infection or inflammation; low can mean immune suppression.
explainer.whatYoursSuggests: Mid-range — a calm, healthy immune baseline.

explainer.whatItIs: The oxygen-carrying protein in red blood cells.
explainer.whyItMatters: Low means anemia (fatigue, breathlessness); high can mean dehydration or other issues.
explainer.whatYoursSuggests: Healthy — good oxygen-carrying capacity.

explainer.whatItIs: The proportion of your blood made up of red cells.
explainer.whyItMatters: Tracks with hemoglobin and hydration status.
explainer.whatYoursSuggests: Mid-range and consistent with the healthy hemoglobin.

explainer.whatItIs: Cell fragments that clot blood and stop bleeding.
explainer.whyItMatters: Out-of-range counts affect bleeding and clotting risk.
explainer.whatYoursSuggests: Normal — healthy clotting capacity.

explainer.whatItIs: How acidic or alkaline your urine is.
explainer.whyItMatters: Shifts with diet and hydration; extremes can relate to stone risk.
explainer.whatYoursSuggests: Mildly acidic and entirely normal.

explainer.whatItIs: A check for protein leaking into the urine.
explainer.whyItMatters: Protein in urine can be an early kidney-stress signal.
explainer.whatYoursSuggests: Negative — no protein detected, consistent with the healthy kidney markers.
